title: Financial Databases: SQL Is Not the Only Option – From ACID Theory to Banking Reality
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
A persistent belief in software architecture circles is that you must use a SQL database for financial applications because relational systems were “designed from the ground up” to support ACID transactions.

In academic courses, ACID is often explained using a highly simplified bank transfer example:

  • Debit one account, credit another — in a single atomic operation.
  • No intermediate states are visible to any user.
  • Total balances remain correct at all times.

It’s an elegant picture. On the whiteboard, you draw a single cylinder representing “the database,” and all updates happen inside it.

In the real world, banking is very different.

Case 1: ATM Cash Withdrawal

Charlie inserts his card into an ATM to withdraw $100. Behind the scenes:

  1. The system checks his account balance.
  2. Confirms it’s at least $100.
  3. Debits his account by $100.
  4. Updates the ATM’s cash inventory to deduct a $100 bill.
  5. Moves the bill to the dispensing slot.
  6. At the exact moment the cash dispenser shutter opens, the withdrawal is considered complete.

In theory, ACID ensures that if any step fails, it’s as if nothing happened: the account remains unchanged, the ATM still contains the bill, and there is no mismatch between the cash dispensed and the account balance.

In reality, ATM transactions span multiple systems — the core banking ledger, ATM controller software, ATM hardware, and interbank ATM networks. Each has its own data store and transaction boundaries. No bank runs this as “one giant SQL transaction” from card swipe to shutter opening.

Case 2: Cross‑Currency Transfer

While traveling in the United States, Charlie’s $100 ATM withdrawal fails because there are no funds in his USD account. He calls his wife, Alice, in Switzerland, and asks her to transfer money from their CHF account to the USD account.

From a database perspective, the CHF‑to‑USD transfer is an ACID operation:

  • Debit the CHF account.
  • Credit the USD account.
  • Apply the correct CHF/USD exchange rate — read once and hold constant for the transaction.

A repeatable read isolation level ensures the exchange rate remains the same throughout.

But isolation levels affect what Charlie sees. With serializable isolation, it’s possible that, when Alice says “done,” Charlie's retry may still see the old balance, depending on transaction ordering. With linearizable (external consistency), confirmation guarantees immediate visibility.

Again, this operation in production is not a single monolithic SQL transaction but spans two accounts across different currency ledgers — often in other databases, possibly even across various data centers or countries.

Case 3: Interbank Card Payment Clearing

Charlie pays for dinner in New York using his Swiss debit card. At the restaurant’s POS terminal:

  • An ISO 8583 authorization request is sent through the payment network.
  • The bank checks Charlie’s available balance.
  • Places a hold for the transaction amount.
  • Sends an approval code back to the merchant.

No money moves at this stage. Overnight, the payment network sends a settlement batch to Charlie’s bank:

  • The hold is released.
  • Funds are debited from Charlie’s account.
  • Funds are credited to the merchant’s bank via interbank transfer.

These are multiple short transactions across different systems — merchant acquirer, card network, issuing bank, settlement processor. Idempotency and reconciliation ensure correctness. There is never a single long-running SQL transaction that covers both authorization and settlement.

Reality Check: How Financial Systems Actually Work

Across all three examples:

  • Financial processes are business transactions composed of multiple short, atomic database transactions.
  • Systems are distributed, often spanning different institutions.
  • Operations are asynchronous, coordinated through messaging and batch processing.
  • Correctness comes from idempotent operations, reconciliation, and consistent reads, not long-lived locks.
  • The available balance for users is typically computed on read as the actual ledger balance minus the sum of pending holds/operations.

Why MongoDB Fits This Reality

The “SQL-or-Nothing” view assumes that financial applications run on a single database node and use a single, long, serializable transaction per operation. That’s not how production systems work.

MongoDB’s architectural model aligns with the realities of modern finance:

  • Many operations are single-document writes — atomic, idempotent, and retried automatically on conflict or failure.
  • Ledger updates can use multi-document ACID transactions, kept short to avoid network and user latency.
  • Reads can use a majority write concern (the default) with a snapshot read concern to ensure consistent data across distributed replicas.
  • MongoDB supports distributed ACID transactions across replica sets and shard clusters — capabilities that are possible in traditional RDBMSs via mechanisms such as XA/two‑phase commit, but often limited in scalability and operational simplicity.

Conclusion

Academic ACID examples make financial operations look like long, interactive, serializable SQL transactions. In reality, banks break these into smaller, discrete transactions, coordinate them asynchronously, and apply strong consistency guarantees only where needed.

MongoDB delivers ACID transactions — single‑document and multi‑document — across a globally distributed architecture. When systems are designed around actual financial workflows, MongoDB fits naturally. SQL is no longer banking’s sole preserve: many fintechs and challenger banks run transactional workloads on MongoDB. NoSQL is also gaining traction for customer data, fraud detection, and even parts of core banking — particularly where flexibility, rapid iteration, and horizontal scalability are critical.
